title: Concurrency & workers
lede: Real OS threads with cross-thread messaging, offered under two surfaces at once: Node's worker_threads and the browser Worker/onmessage shape. The pervasive divergence is rigidity: messaging is statically typed and monomorphic — one message type per direction, one listener per event, arrow-function literals only — and worker paths must be string literals because each worker file compiles into the same binary as its own entry function. Payloads are structured-clone-safe values (no arrays through onmessage), with SharedArrayBuffer/Atomics and MessagePort crossing by reference for shared-memory work.

entries.name: Worker
entries.signature: new Worker(path: string, opts?: { workerData?: T }): Worker
entries.description: Spawns a real OS thread running a worker module, exposing both the Node worker_threads API (w.on('message', ...), import { Worker } from 'worker_threads') and the ambient browser shape (new Worker, w.onmessage, e.data). The worker file compiles into the same binary as its own entry function; each thread runs its own event loop with thread-local runtime singletons, and messages travel over pipes as pointer envelopes deep-copied at the boundary. SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics (add/load/wait/notify/isLockFree) give lock-free shared-memory counters without messages carrying the value.

params.name: path
params.desc: String literal path to the worker module.

params.name: opts
params.desc: Optional initial data (structured-clone-safe, or a SharedArrayBuffer/MessagePort by reference).

returns.desc: A handle exposing postMessage, on/onmessage, and terminate.

differences: One listener per event, arrow-function literals only
One message type per direction, declared by annotation
Payloads: structured-clone-safe values only (plus `SharedArrayBuffer`/`MessagePort`, which cross by reference); strings share their buffer across threads; no arrays through `onmessage`/`e.data`
`'error'` carries the message string, not an Error object; no `self.onerror`
`terminate()` is cooperative, keeps queued messages, always exits 1
Worker path must be a string literal; a worker module can't also be imported, can't spawn workers, and its named functions can't read its own top-level bindings
`-mm=manual` leaks per message; no combining with `http.listen({workers:N})`

entries.name: BroadcastChannel
entries.description: Name-keyed pub/sub across threads via a process-wide registry: every subscriber to a channel name gets its own deep copy of each posted message (a synthesized clone thunk, called once per subscriber). Delivery rides each thread's select() loop over per-endpoint pipes, works same-thread and across workers, and a registered onmessage holds its thread's loop alive until close() (Node ref semantics).

params.name: name
params.desc: String literal channel name; fixes one message type program-wide.

returns.desc: An endpoint with postMessage, onmessage, and close.

entries.snippet:
const bc = new BroadcastChannel('news');
setTimeout(() => { bc.postMessage("markets up in Thessaloniki"); }, 100);
differences: Channel name must be a string literal; one message type per channel name, program-wide (first `postMessage` or annotated `onmessage` fixes it)
`onmessage` property only (arrow-function literal, `(e: { data: T })`); no `addEventListener`, no `'messageerror'`
`close()` leaks the endpoint's two pipe fds by design (closes a race against an in-flight post)
`-mm=manual` leaks per delivery (payload ownership passes to the listener)

entries.name: MessageChannel / MessagePort
entries.signature: new MessageChannel<T = number>(): { port1: MessagePort<T>, port2: MessagePort<T> }
entries.description: A typed port pair whose two ports talk directly over one shared endpoint runtime (a pipe per endpoint, peer-linked halves). A port crosses a worker boundary whole — as workerData or as an entire postMessage payload — and is shared, not neutered: the sender must stop using a sent port. Whichever thread registers a port's onmessage drains it, so no adoption protocol is needed when a port moves to a worker. Importable under Node's module name (import { MessageChannel, MessagePort, BroadcastChannel } from 'worker_threads').

params.name: T
params.desc: Message type fixed at construction (default number), symmetric for both ports.

differences: Message type fixed at construction (`new MessageChannel<T>()`, default `number`), symmetric for both ports

A port crosses a worker boundary only whole — as `workerData` or as the entire `postMessage` payload — and is **shared, not neutered**: the sender must stop using a sent port (unsynchronized use from two threads is memory-safe but unordered); the `MessageChannel` pair box itself never crosses
`onmessage` property only (arrow literal); no `on('message')`, no `start()`/`'close'` event, no array payloads via `onmessage`
`close()` leaks two pipe fds; `-mm=manual` leaks per message

entries.name: klain:sync goroutines, channels, select
entries.statusRow: klain:sync goroutines, channels, select (go, Channel<T>, select)
entries.signature: import { go, Channel, select, defaultCase } from 'klain:sync'; go(fn: () => void); new Channel<T>(capacity?); select(...cases)
entries.description: An explicitly-non-Node opt-in: Go's concurrency model, not a JS approximation. go(fn) spawns a cheap goroutine onto a GMP work-stealing scheduler (one logical processor + pinned OS thread per GOMAXPROCS, global run-queue backstop, half-queue stealing) in an embedded C runtime linked only when klain:sync is imported. Channel<T> is a Go channel: synchronous blocking send/receive (not await) that parks the goroutine — the OS thread keeps running others — as an unbuffered rendezvous or buffered ring, with close() and `for (const v of ch)` range. select(...) is Go's random-fair select over recvCase/sendCase/defaultCase. Cooperative preemption is complete: a sysmon thread flags an over-budget goroutine and compiler-inserted safepoints at every function entry and loop back-edge yield it, so no goroutine can starve the others.

params.name: fn
params.desc: go(fn): the goroutine body; captures channels from its enclosing scope.

params.name: capacity
params.desc: new Channel<T>(capacity): 0/omitted is an unbuffered rendezvous; >0 is a buffered ring.

params.name: ...cases
params.desc: select(...): ch.recvCase(handler) / ch.sendCase(value, handler) / defaultCase(handler); runs one ready case, or blocks until one fires (unless a defaultCase is present).

returns.desc: go returns nothing; new Channel<T> returns a channel with .send(v: T)/.receive(): T/.close().

differences: Channel ops are synchronous blocking, not await; the element is a fixed 8-byte slot (number/string/object/boolean).

select cases are ch.recvCase(v => ...) / ch.sendCase(x, () => ...) / defaultCase(() => ...); a recv handler gets the value but not the closed flag — use the for-of range (which ends on close) to detect it.

Fixed goroutine stacks (default 256 KiB, tunable via KLAINSYNC_STACK_KB); true growable/moving stacks are gated on precise stack maps. Blocking-syscall P-handoff is a bounded sysmon rescue-M approximation. send-after-close / double-close abort the process (Go-panic parity); native-only.
